entries.c3b8fba5febe851ebc55a61a623fba45a1bf3f41: <div sID="gen20806" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Zech.4" sID="Zech.4"/> <div eID="gen20806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20807" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20808" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have another comfortable vision, which, as it was explained to the prophet, had much in it for the encouragement of the people of God in their present straits, which were so great that they thought their case helpless, that their temple could never be rebuilt nor their city replenished; and therefore the scope of the vision is to show that God would, by his own power, perfect the work, though the assistance given to it by its friends were ever so weak, and the resistance given to it by its enemies were ever so strong. Here is, I. The awakening of the prophet to observe the vision, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. The vision itself, of a candlestick with seven lamps, which were supplied with oil, and kept burning, immediately from two olive-trees that grew by it, one on either side, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.2-Zech.2.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. III. The general encouragement hereby intended to be given to the builders of the temple to go on in that good work, assuring them that it should be brought to perfection at last, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.4-Zech.2.10">ver. 4-10</reference>. IV. The particular explication of the vision, for the illustration of these assurances, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.11-Zech.2.14">ver. 11-14</reference>.
entries.5f567c2618b719b66494281fae7fceb54c201991: <div eID="gen20808" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20807" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Golden Candlestick; The Building of the Temple Encouraged. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  520.)</title> <div sID="gen20809" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the angel that talked with me came again, and waked me, as a man that is wakened out of his sleep, <hi type="super">2</hi> And said unto me, What seest thou? And I said, I have looked, and behold a candlestick all <hi type="italic">of</hi> gold, with a bowl upon the top of it, and his seven lamps thereon, and seven pipes to the seven lamps, which <hi type="italic">are</hi> upon the top thereof: <hi type="super">3</hi> And two olive trees by it, one upon the right <hi type="italic">side</hi> of the bowl, and the other upon the left <hi type="italic">side</hi> thereof. <hi type="super">4</hi> So I answered and spake to the angel that talked with me, saying, What <hi type="italic">are</hi> these, my lord? <hi type="super">5</hi> Then the angel that talked with me answered and said unto me, Knowest thou not what these be? And I said, No, my lord. <hi type="super">6</hi> Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <hi type="super">7</hi> Who <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel <hi type="italic">thou shalt become</hi> a plain: and he shall bring forth the headstone <hi type="italic">thereof with</hi> shoutings, <hi type="italic">crying,</hi> Grace, grace unto it. <hi type="super">8</hi> Moreover the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">9</hi> The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it; and thou shalt know that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts hath sent me unto you. <hi type="super">10</hi> For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel <hi type="italic">with</hi> those seven; they <hi type="italic">are</hi> the eyes of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which run to and fro through the whole earth. <div eID="gen20809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20810" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The prophet prepared to receive the discovery that was to be made to him: <hi type="italic">The angel that talked with him came and waked him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.4.1">v. 1</reference>. It seems, though he was in conference with an angel, and about matters of great and public concern, yet he grew dull and fell asleep, as it should seem, while the angel was yet talking with him. Thus the disciples, when they saw Christ transfigured, were <hi type="italic">heavy with sleep,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.9.32">Luke ix. 32</reference>. The prophet's spirit, no doubt, was willing to attend to that which was to be seen and heard, but the flesh was weak; his body could not keep pace with his soul in divine contemplations; the strangeness of the visions perhaps stupefied him, and so he was overcome with sleep, or perhaps the sweetness of the visions composed him and even sung him asleep. Daniel was in a <hi type="italic">deep sleep when he heard the voice of the angel's words,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.10.9">Dan. x. 9</reference>. We shall never be fit for converse with spirits till we have got clear of these bodies of flesh. It should seem, the angel let him lose himself a little, that he might be fresh to receive new discoveries, but then <hi type="italic">waked him,</hi> to his surprise, <hi type="italic">as a man that is wakened out of his sleep.</hi> Note, We need the Spirit of God, not only to make known to us divine things, but to make us take notice of them. <hi type="italic">He wakens morning by morning, he wakens my ear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.50.4">Isa. l. 4</reference>. We should beg of God that, whenever he speaks to us, he would awaken us, and we should then <hi type="italic">stir up ourselves.</hi> <div eID="gen20810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20811" type="x-p"/> II. The discovery that was made to him when he was thus prepared. The angel asked him, <hi type="italic">What seest thou?</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.4.2">v. 2</reference>. When he was awake perhaps he would not have taken notice of what was presented to his view if he had not thus been excited to look about him. When he observed he saw a <hi type="italic">golden candlestick,</hi> such a one as was in the temple formerly, and with the like this temple should in due time be furnished. The church is a candlestick, set up for the enlightening of this dark world and the holding forth of the light of divine revelation to it. The candle is God's; the church is but the candlestick, but all of gold, denoting the great worth and excellence of the church of God. This golden candlestick had <hi type="italic">seven lamps</hi> branching out from it, so many sockets, in each of which was a burning and shining light. The Jewish church was but one, and though the Jews that were dispersed, it is probable, had synagogues in other countries, yet they were but as so many lamps belonging to one candlestick; but now, under the gospel, Christ is the centre of unity, and not Jerusalem, or any one place; and therefore seven particular churches are represented, not as <hi type="italic">seven lamps,</hi> but as seven several <hi type="italic">golden candlesticks,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.20">Rev. i. 20</reference>. This candlestick had one <hi type="italic">bowl,</hi> or common receiver, on the top, into which oil was continually dropping, and from it, by seven secret pipes, or passages, it was diffused to the seven lamps, so that, without any further care, they received oil as fast as they wasted it (as in those which we call <hi type="italic">fountain-ink-horns,</hi> or <hi type="italic">fountain-pens</hi>); they never wanted, nor were ever glutted, and so kept always burning clear. And the bowl too was continually supplied, without any care or attendance of man; for (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.3">v. 3</reference>) he saw <hi type="italic">two olive-trees,</hi> one on each side the candlestick, that were so fat and fruitful that of their own accord they poured plenty of oil continually into the bowl, which by two larger pipes (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.12">v. 12</reference>) dispersed the oil to smaller ones and so to the lamps; so that nobody needed to attend this candlestick, to furnish it with oil (it tarried not for man, nor waited for the sons of men), the scope of which is to show that God easily can, and often does, accomplish his gracious purposes concerning his church by his own wisdom and power, without any art or labour of man, and that though sometimes he makes use of instruments, yet he neither needs them nor is tied to them, but can do his work without them, and will rather than it shall be undone. <div eID="gen20811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20812" type="x-p"/> III. The enquiry which the prophet made concerning the meaning of this, and the gentle reproof given him for his dulness (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">I answered and spoke to the angel,</hi> saying, <hi type="italic">What are these, my lord?</hi> Observe how respectfully he speaks to the angel; he calls him <hi type="italic">my lord.</hi> Those that would be taught must give honour to their teachers. He saw what these <hi type="italic">were,</hi> but asked what these <hi type="italic">signified.</hi> Note, It is very desirable to know the meaning of God's manifestations of himself and his mind both in his word and by his ordinances and providences. <hi type="italic">What mean you by these</hi> services, by these signs? And those that would understand the mind of God must be inquisitive. <hi type="italic">Then shall we know if we follow on to know,</hi> if we not only <hi type="italic">hear,</hi> but, as Christ, <hi type="italic">ask questions</hi> upon what we hear, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.46">Luke ii. 46</reference>. The angel answered him with a question, <hi type="italic">Knowest thou not what these be?</hi> intimating that if he had considered, and compared spiritual things with spiritual, he might have guessed at the meaning of these things; for he knew that there was a golden candlestick in the tabernacle, which it was the priests' constant business to supply with oil and to keep burning, for the use of the tabernacle; when therefore he saw, in vision, such a candlestick, with lamps always kept burning, and yet no priests to attend it, nor any occasion for them, he might discern the meaning of this to be that though God had set up the priesthood again, yet he could carry on his own work for and in his people without them. Note, We have reason to be ashamed of ourselves that we do not more readily apprehend the meaning of divine discoveries. The angel asked the prophet this question, to draw from him an acknowledgment of his own dulness, and darkness, and slowness to understand, and he had it immediately: "<hi type="italic">I said, No, my lord;</hi> I know not what these are." Visions had their significance, but often dark and hard to be understood, and the prophets themselves were not always aware of it at first. But those that would be taught of God must see and acknowledge their own ignorance, and their need to be taught, and must apply to God for instruction. To him that gave us the cabinet we must apply for the key wherewith to unlock it. God will teach the meek and humble, not those that are conceited of themselves and lean on the broken reed of their own understanding. <div eID="gen20812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20813" type="x-p"/> IV. The general intention of this vision. Without a critical descant upon every circumstance of the vision, the design of it is to assure the prophet, and by him the people, that this good work of building the temple should, by the special care of divine Providence, and the immediate influence of divine grace, be brought to a happy issue, though the enemies of it were many and mighty and the friends and furtherers of it few and feeble. Note, In the explication of visions and parables, we must look at the principal scope of them, and be satisfied with that, if that be clear, though we may not be able to account for every circumstance, or accommodate it to our purpose. The angel lets the prophet know, in general, that this vision was designed to illustrate a word which the Lord had to say to Zerubbabel, to encourage him to go on with the building of the temple. Let him know that he is a worker together with God in it, and that it is a work which God will own and crown. <div eID="gen20813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20814" type="x-p"/> 1. God will carry on and complete this work, as he had begun their deliverance from Babylon, not by external force, but by secret operations and internal influences upon the minds of men. <hi type="italic">He</hi> says this who is the <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts,</hi> and could do it <hi type="italic">vi et armis—by force,</hi> has legions at command; but he will do it, <hi type="italic">not by</hi> human <hi type="italic">might or power,</hi> but <hi type="italic">by his own Spirit.</hi> What is done by his Spirit is done by might and power, but it stands in opposition to visible force. Israel was brought out of Egypt, and into Canaan, by might and power; in both these works of wonder great slaughter was made. But they were brought out of Babylon, and into Canaan the second time, <hi type="italic">by the Spirit of the Lord of hosts</hi> working upon the spirit of Cyrus, and inclining him to proclaim liberty to them, and working upon the spirits of the captives, and inclining them to accept the liberty offered them. It was by the <hi type="italic">Spirit of the Lord of hosts</hi> that the people were excited and animated to build the temple; and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> they are said to be <hi type="italic">helped by the prophets of God,</hi> because they, as the Spirit's mouth, spoke to their hearts, <reference osisRef="Ezra.5.2">Ezra v. 2</reference>. It was by the same Spirit that the heart of Darius was inclined to favour and further that good work and that the sworn enemies of it were infatuated in their councils, so that they could not hinder it as they designed. Note, The work of God is often carried on very successfully when yet it is carried on very silently, and without the assistance of human force; the gospel-temple is built, not by might or power (for <hi type="italic">the weapons of our warfare are not carnal</hi>), but by the <hi type="italic">Spirit of the Lord of hosts,</hi> whose work on men's consciences is mighty to the pulling down of strong-holds; thus the excellency of the power is of God, and not of man. When instruments fail, let us therefore leave it to God to do his work himself by his own Spirit. <div eID="gen20814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20815" type="x-p"/> 2. All the difficulties and oppositions that lie in the way shall be got over and removed, even those that seem insuperable (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who art thou, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain.</hi> See here, (1.) How the difficulty is represented; it is a <hi type="italic">great mountain,</hi> impassable and immovable, a heap of rubbish, like a great mountain, which must be got away, or the work cannot go on. The enemies of the Jews are proud and hard as great mountains; but, when God has work to do, the mountains that stand in the way of it shall dwindle into mole-hills; for see here, (2.) How these difficulties are despised: "<hi type="italic">Who art thou, O great mountain!</hi> that thou shouldst stand in God's way and think to stop the progress of his work? Who art thou that lookest so big, that thus threatenest, and art thus feared? <hi type="italic">Before Zerubbabel,</hi> when he is God's agent, <hi type="italic">thou shalt become a plain.</hi> All the difficulties shall vanish, and all the objections be got over. <hi type="italic">Every mountain and hill</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">brought low</hi> when the <hi type="italic">way of the Lord</hi> is to be <hi type="italic">prepared,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.40.4">Isa. xl. 4</reference>. Faith will remove mountains and make them plains. Christ is our Zerubbabel; mountains of difficulty were in the way of his undertaking, but before him they were all levelled; nothing is too hard for his grace to do. <div eID="gen20815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20816" type="x-p"/> 3. The same hand that has begun this good work will perform it: <hi type="italic">He shall bring forth the head-stone</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.7">v. 7</reference>); and again (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house,</hi> be it spoken to his honour (perhaps with his own hands he laid the first stone), and though it has been long retarded, and is still much opposed, yet it shall be finished at last; he shall live to see it finished, nay, and <hi type="italic">his hands shall also finish it;</hi> herein he is a type of Christ, who is both the <hi type="italic">author</hi> and the <hi type="italic">finisher of our faith;</hi> and his being the <hi type="italic">author</hi> of it is an assurance to us that he will be the <hi type="italic">finisher,</hi> for, <hi type="italic">as for God, his work is perfect;</hi> has he begun and shall he not make an end? Zerubbabel shall himself <hi type="italic">bring forth the head-stone with shoutings,</hi> and loud acclamations of joy, among the spectators. The acclamations are not <hi type="italic">huzzas,</hi> but <hi type="italic">Grace, grace;</hi> that is the burden of the triumphant songs which the church sings. It may be taken, (1.) As magnifying free grace, and giving to that all the glory of what is done. When the work is finished it must be thankfully acknowledged that it was not by any policy or power of our own that it was brought to perfection, but that it was grace that did it—God's good-will towards us and his good work in us and for us. <hi type="italic">Grace, grace,</hi> must be cried, not only to the head-stone, but to the foundation-stone, the corner-stone, and indeed to every stone in God's building; from first to last it is nothing of works, but all of grace, and all our crowns must be cast at the feet of free grace. <hi type="italic">Not unto us, O Lord! not unto us.</hi> (2.) As depending upon free grace, and desiring the continuance of it, for what is yet to be done. <hi type="italic">Grace, grace,</hi> is the language of prayer as well as of praise; now that this building is finished, all happiness attend it! Peace be within its walls, and, in order to that, <hi type="italic">grace.</hi> Let the beauty of the Lord our God be upon it! Note, What comes from the grace of God may, in faith, and upon good grounds, be committed to the grace of God, for God will not forsake the work of his own hands. <div eID="gen20816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20817" type="x-p"/> 4. This shall be a full ratification of the prophecies which went before concerning the Jews' return, and their settlement again. When the temple is finished then <hi type="italic">thou shalt know that the Lord of hosts has sent me unto you.</hi> Note, The exact accomplishment of scripture prophecies is a convincing proof of their divine original. Thus God <hi type="italic">confirms the word of his servant,</hi> by <hi type="italic">saying to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be built,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.26">Isa. xliv. 26</reference>. No word of God shall fall to the ground, nor shall there fail one iota or tittle of it. Zechariah's prophecies of the approaching day of deliverance to the church would soon appear, by the accomplishment of them, to be of God. <div eID="gen20817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20818" type="x-p"/> 5. This shall effectually silence those that looked with contempt upon the beginning of this work, <reference osisRef="Zech.4.10">v. 10</reference>. Who, where, is he now that despised the day of small things, and thought this work would never come to any thing? The Jews themselves despised the foundation of the second temple, because it was likely to be so far inferior to the first, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.12">Ezra iii. 12</reference>. Their enemies despised the wall when it was in the building, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.19">Neh. ii. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.4.2-Neh.4.3">iv. 2, 3</reference>. But let them not do it. Note, In God's work the day of small things is not to be despised. Though the instruments be weak and unlikely, God often chooses such, by them to bring about great things. As a great mountain becomes a plain before him when he pleases, so a little stone, cut out of a mountain without hands, comes to fill the earth, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.35">Dan. ii. 35</reference>. Though the beginnings be small, God can make the latter end greatly to increase; a grain of mustard-seed may become a great tree. Let not the dawning light be despised, for it will shine more and more to the perfect day. The day of small things is the day of precious things, and will be the day of great things. <div eID="gen20818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20819" type="x-p"/> 6. This shall abundantly satisfy all the hearty well-wishers to God's interest, who will be glad to see themselves mistaken in <hi type="italic">despising the day of small things.</hi> Those that despaired of the finishing of the work shall rejoice when they <hi type="italic">see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel,</hi> when they see him busy among the builders, giving orders and directions what to do, and taking care that the work be done with great exactness, that it may be both fine and firm. Note, It is matter of great rejoicing to all good people to see magistrates careful and active for the edifying of the house of God, to see the plummet in the hand of those who have power to do much, if they have but a heart according to it; we see not Zerubbabel with the trowel in his hand (that is left to the workmen, the ministers), but we see him with the plummet in his hand, and it is no disparagement, but an honour to him. Magistrates are to inspect ministers' work, and to speak comfortably to the Levites that do their duty. <div eID="gen20819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20820" type="x-p"/> 7. This shall highly magnify the wisdom and care of God's providence, which is always employed for the good of his church. Zerubbabel does his part, does as much as man can do to forward the work, but it is <hi type="italic">with those seven, those seven eyes of the Lord</hi> which we read of <reference osisRef="Zech.3.9">ch. iii. 9</reference>. He could do nothing if the watchful, powerful, gracious providence of God did not go before him and go along with him in it. Except the Lord had built this house, Zerubbabel and the rest would have <hi type="italic">laboured in vain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.127.1">Ps. cxxvii. 1</reference>. These <hi type="italic">eyes of the Lord</hi> are those that <hi type="italic">run to and fro through the whole earth,</hi> that take cognizance of all the creatures and all their actions (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">2 Chron. xvi. 9</reference>), and inspire and direct all, according to the divine counsels. Note, We must not think that God is so taken up with the affairs of his church as to neglect the world; but it is a comfort to us that the same all-wise almighty Providence that governs the nations of the earth is in a particular manner conversant about the church. Those <hi type="italic">seven eyes</hi> that <hi type="italic">run through the earth</hi> are all <hi type="italic">upon the stone</hi> that Zerubbabel is laying straight with his plummet, to see that it be well laid. And those that have the plummet in their hand must look up to <hi type="italic">those eyes of the Lord,</hi> must have a constant regard to divine Providence, and act in dependence upon its guidance and submission to its disposals.
entries.e85d52ce98522723f913cfbe805fe65199fa35ef: <div eID="gen20820" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Olive-Trees. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 520.)</title> <div sID="gen20821" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Then answered I, and said unto him, What <hi type="italic">are</hi> these two olive trees upon the right <hi type="italic">side</hi> of the candlestick and upon the left <hi type="italic">side</hi> thereof? <hi type="super">12</hi> And I answered again, and said unto him, What <hi type="italic">be these</hi> two olive branches which through the two golden pipes empty the golden <hi type="italic">oil</hi> out of themselves? <hi type="super">13</hi> And he answered me and said, Knowest thou not what these <hi type="italic">be?</hi> And I said, No, my lord. <hi type="super">14</hi> Then said he, These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the two anointed ones, that stand by the Lord of the whole earth. <div eID="gen20821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20822" type="x-p"/> Enough is said to Zechariah to encourage him, and to enable him to encourage others, with reference to the good work of building the temple which they were now about, and that was the principal intention of the vision he saw; but still he is inquisitive about the particulars, which we will ascribe, not to any vain curiosity, but to the value he had for divine discoveries and the pleasure he took in acquainting himself with them. Those that know much of the things of God cannot but have a humble desire to know more. Now observe, <div eID="gen20822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20823" type="x-p"/> I. What his enquiry was. He understood the meaning of the candlestick with its lamps: It is Jerusalem, it is the temple, and their salvation that is to <hi type="italic">go forth as a lamp that burns;</hi> but he wants to know what are these <hi type="italic">two olive-trees</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.11">v. 11</reference>), these <hi type="italic">two olive-branches?</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.4.12">v. 12</reference>. Observe here, 1. He asked. Note, Those that would be acquainted with the things of God must be inquisitive concerning those things. Ask, and you shall be told. 2. He asked twice, his first question having no reply given to it. Note, If satisfactory answers be not given to our enquiries and requests quickly, we must renew them, and repeat them, and continue instant and importunate in them, and the vision shall at length <hi type="italic">speak, and not lie.</hi> 3. His second query varied somewhat from the former. He first asked, What are <hi type="italic">these two olive-trees,</hi> but afterwards, <hi type="italic">What are these two olive-branches?</hi> that is, those boughs of the tree that hung over the bowl and distilled oil into it. When we enquire concerning the grace of God, it must be rather as it is communicated to us by the fruitful boughs of the word and ordinances (for that is one of the <hi type="italic">things revealed,</hi> which <hi type="italic">belong to us and to our children</hi>) than as it is resident in the good olive where all our springs are, for that is one of the <hi type="italic">secret things,</hi> which <hi type="italic">belong not to us.</hi> 4. In his enquiry he mentioned the observations he had made upon the vision; he took notice not only of what was obvious at first sight, that the two olive-trees grew, one <hi type="italic">on the right side and the other on the left side of the candlestick</hi> (so nigh, so ready, is divine grace to the church), but he observed further, upon a more narrow inspection, that the <hi type="italic">two olive-branches,</hi> from which in particular the candlestick did receive of <hi type="italic">the root and fatness of the olive</hi> (as the apostle says of the church, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.17">Rom. xi. 17</reference>), did empty the <hi type="italic">golden oil</hi> (that is, the clear bright oil, the best in its kind, and of great value, as if it were <hi type="italic">aurum potabile—liquid gold) out of themselves through the two golden pipes,</hi> or (as the margin reads it) which <hi type="italic">by the hand of the two golden pipes empty out of themselves oil into the gold,</hi> that is, into the <hi type="italic">golden bowl</hi> on the head of the candlestick. Our Lord Jesus emptied himself, to fill us; his precious blood is the golden oil in which we are supplied with all we need. <div eID="gen20823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20824" type="x-p"/> II. What answer was given to his enquiry. Now again the angel obliged him expressly to own his ignorance, before he informed him (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Knowest thou not what these are?</hi> If thou knowest the church to be the candlestick, canst thou think the olive-trees, that supply it with oil, to be any other than the grace of God?" But he owned he either did not fully understand it or was afraid he did not rightly understand it: <hi type="italic">I said, No, my Lord, how should I, except some one guide me?</hi> And then he told him (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">These are the two sons of oil</hi> (so it is in the original), <hi type="italic">the two anointed ones</hi> (so we read it), rather, <hi type="italic">the two oily ones.</hi> That which we read (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.1">Isa. v. 1</reference>) a <hi type="italic">very fruitful hill</hi> is in the original <hi type="italic">the horn of the son of oil,</hi> a fat and fattening soil. 1. If by the candlestick we understand the visible church, particularly that of the Jews at that time, for whose comfort it was primarily intended, these <hi type="italic">sons of oil,</hi> that <hi type="italic">stand before the Lord of the whole earth,</hi> are the two great ordinances and offices of the magistracy and ministry, at that time lodged in the hands of those two great and good men Zerubbabel and Joshua. Kings and priests were anointed; this prince, this priest, were <hi type="italic">oily ones,</hi> endued with the gifts and graces of God's Spirit, to qualify them for the work to which they were called. They <hi type="italic">stood before the Lord of the whole earth,</hi> to minister to him, and to receive direction from him; and a great influence they had upon the affairs of the church at that time. Their wisdom, courage, and zeal, were continually emptying themselves into the golden bowl, to keep the lamps burning; and, when they are gone, others shall be raised up to carry on the same work; Israel shall no longer be without prince and priest. Good magistrates and good ministers that are themselves anointed with the grace of God and <hi type="italic">stand by the Lord of the whole earth,</hi> as faithful adherents to his cause, contribute very much to the maintaining and advancing of religion and the shining forth of the word of life. 2. If by the candlestick we understand the church of the first-born, of true believers, these sons of oil may be meant of Christ and the Spirit, the Redeemer and the Comforter. Christ is not only the Messiah, the <hi type="italic">Anointed One</hi> himself, but he is the <hi type="italic">good olive</hi> to his church; and <hi type="italic">from his fulness we receive,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.16">John i. 16</reference>. And the Holy Spirit is the <hi type="italic">unction or anointing</hi> which we have received, <reference osisRef="1John.2.20">1 John ii. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.2.27">27</reference>. From Christ, the <hi type="italic">olive tree,</hi> by the <hi type="italic">Spirit, the olive branch,</hi> all the golden oil of grace is communicated to believers, which keeps their lamps burning, and without a constant supply of which they would soon go out. They <hi type="italic">stand by the Lord of the whole earth,</hi> who is in a special manner the church's Lord; for the Son was to be sent by the Father, and so was the Holy Ghost, in the time appointed, and they stand by him ready to go.  <chapter eID="Zech.4"/> <div eID="gen20824" type="x-p"/>

entries.eca0548a8ab0dbc88fbbf9be7b8cd4d989a07131: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13053"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Zech.4.1-Zech.4.14">Zec 4:1-14</reference>. Fifth Vision. The golden candlestick and the two olive trees. The temple shall be completed by the aid of God's Spirit.</title> <div sID="gen24522" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13053"/><hi type="bold">1. waked me--</hi>The prophet was lying in a state of ecstatic slumber with astonishment at the previous vision. "Came again, and waked me," does not imply that the angel had departed and now returned, but is an idiom for "waked me again." <div eID="gen24522" type="x-p"/>
entries.3266d6361a4b7d1b58cf6e290c7ddacdbbb4c845: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13054"/><div sID="gen24523" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13054"/><hi type="bold">2. candlestick--</hi>symbolizing the Jewish theocracy; and ultimately, the Church of which the Jewish portion is to be the head: the light-bearer (so the original is of "lights," <reference osisRef="Matt.5.14">Mt 5:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.15">Php 2:15</reference>) to the world.<div eID="gen24523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24524" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ... gold--</hi>all pure in doctrine and practice, precious and indestructible; such is the true ideal of the Church; such she shall be (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.13">Psa 45:13</reference>).<div eID="gen24524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24525" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bowl upon the top--</hi>In the candlestick of the tabernacle the plural is used, bowls (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.31">Ex 25:31</reference>). The Hebrew implies that it was the fountain of supply of oil to the lamps. Christ at the head ("on the top") of the Church is the true fountain, of whose fulness of the Spirit all we receive grace (<reference osisRef="John.1.16">Joh 1:16</reference>).<div eID="gen24525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24526" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his seven lamps--</hi>united in one stem; so in <reference osisRef="Exod.25.32">Ex 25:32</reference>. But in <reference osisRef="Rev.1.12">Re 1:12</reference> the seven candlesticks are separate. The Gentile churches will not realize their unity till the Jewish Church as the stem unites all the lamps in one candlestick (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.16-Rom.11.24">Ro 11:16-24</reference>). The "seven lamps," in <reference osisRef="Rev.4.5">Re 4:5</reference>, are the "seven Spirits of God."<div eID="gen24526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seven pipes--</hi>feeding tubes, seven apiece from the "bowl" to each lamp (see Margin) [Maurer and Calvin]; literally, "seven and seven": forty-nine in all. The greater the number of oil-feeding pipes, the brighter the light of the lamps. The explanation in <reference osisRef="Zech.4.6">Zec 4:6</reference> is, that man's power by itself can neither retard nor advance God's work, that the real motive-power is God's Spirit. The seven times seven imply the manifold modes by which the Spirit's grace is imparted to the Church in her manifold work of enlightening the world. <div eID="gen24527" type="x-p"/>
entries.27075240730091b70e86c8b79ab9673576e626a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13055"/><div sID="gen24528" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13055"/><hi type="bold">3. two olive trees--</hi>supplying oil to the bowl. The Holy Ghost, who fills with His fulness Messiah (the anointed: the "bowl"), from whom flow supplies of grace to the Church.<div eID="gen24528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24529" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by it--</hi>literally, "upon it," that is, growing so as somewhat to overtop it. For the explanation of the "two" see <reference osisRef="Zech.4.12">Zec 4:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.4.14">14</reference>. <div eID="gen24529" type="x-p"/>
entries.4952180d23b63540a75010dd98fa198bd2285d06: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13056"/><div sID="gen24530" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13056"/>4. The prophet is instructed in the truths meant, that we may read them with the greater reverence and attention [Calvin]. <div eID="gen24530" type="x-p"/>
entries.b9c6dfa3fe6acfef8e02c106cdc0cf0d806b6298: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13057"/><div sID="gen24531" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13057"/><hi type="bold">5. Knowest thou not, &c.--</hi>Not a reproof of his ignorance, but a stimulus to reflection on the mystery.<div eID="gen24531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24532" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">No, my lord--</hi>ingenious confession of ignorance; as a little child he casts himself for instruction at the feet of the Lord. <div eID="gen24532" type="x-p"/>
entries.0817e0d2b866de8da3f23fb9d32a494e328213d5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13058"/><div sID="gen24533" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13058"/><hi type="bold">6. Not by might ... but by my Spirit--</hi>As the lamps burned continually, supplied with oil from a source (the living olive trees) which man did not make, so Zerubbabel need not be disheartened because of his weakness; for as the work is one to be effected by the living Spirit (compare <reference osisRef="Hag.2.5">Hag 2:5</reference>) of God, man's weakness is no obstacle, for God's might will perfect strength out of weakness (<reference osisRef="Hos.1.7">Ho 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.10">2Co 12:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.34">He 11:34</reference>). "Might and power" express human strength of every description, physical, mental, moral. Or, "might" is the strength of many (an "army," literally); "power," that of one man [Pembellus]. God can save, "whether with many, or with them that have no power" (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.11">2Ch 14:11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.6">1Sa 14:6</reference>). So in the conversion of sinners (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.6">1Co 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.4">2Co 10:4</reference>). "Zerubbabel" is addressed as the chief civil authority in directing the work. <div eID="gen24533" type="x-p"/>
entries.8b700bc20550c6980b6741aa4ca9e82166102448: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13059"/><div sID="gen24534" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13059"/>7. All mountain-like obstacles (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.4">Is 40:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.11">49:11</reference>) in Zerubbabel's way shall be removed, so that the crowning top-stone shall be put on, and the completion of the work be acknowledged as wholly of "grace." Antitypically, the antichristian last foe of Israel, the obstacle preventing her establishment in Palestine, about to be crushed before Messiah, is probably meant (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.25">Jr 51:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.2.34">Da 2:34</reference>, 44; <reference osisRef="Matt.21.44">Mt 21:44</reference>).<div eID="gen24534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24535" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring forth the head-stone--</hi>Primarily, bring it forth from the place where it was chiselled and give it to the workmen to put on the top of the building. It was customary for chief magistrates to lay the foundation, and also the crowning top-stone (compare <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.10">Ezr 3:10</reference>). Antitypically, the reference is to the time when the full number of the spiritual Church shall be completed, and also when "all Israel shall be saved" (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Ro 11:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.40">He 11:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">12:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.4-Rev.7.9">Re 7:4-9</reference>).<div eID="gen24535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24536" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Grace, grace--</hi>The repetition expresses, Grace from first to last (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.3">Is 26:3</reference>, Margin). Thus the Jews are urged to pray perseveringly and earnestly that the same grace which completed it may always preserve it. "Shoutings" of acclamation accompanied the foundation of the literal temple (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.11">Ezr 3:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.13">13</reference>). So shoutings of "Hosanna" greeted the Saviour in entering Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.9">Mt 21:9</reference>), when about to complete the purchase of salvation by His death: His Body being the second temple, or place of God's inhabitation (<reference osisRef="John.2.20">Joh 2:20</reference>, 21). So when the full number of the saints and of Israel is complete, and God shall say, "It is done," then again shall "a great voice of much people in heaven" attribute all to the "grace" of God, saying, "Alleluia! Salvation, and glory, and honor, and power, unto the Lord our God" (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.1">Re 19:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.6">6</reference>). <reference osisRef="Ps.118.22">Psa 118:22</reference> regards Him as "the head-stone of the corner," that is, the foundation-stone. Compare the angels acclamations at His birth, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.14">Lu 2:14</reference>. Here it is the top-stone. Messiah is not only the "Author," but also the Finisher (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.2">He 12:2</reference>). "Grace" is ascribed "unto it," that is, the stone, Messiah. Hence the benediction begins, "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.13.14">2Co 13:14</reference>). <div eID="gen24536" type="x-p"/>
entries.26946bf7aa02069c4922be2b27faee5e0bb1da1f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13060"/><div sID="gen24537" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13060"/><hi type="bold">9. Zerubbabel ... shall ... finish it--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.15">Ezr 6:15</reference>) in the sixth year of Darius' reign.<div eID="gen24537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24538" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord ... sent me unto you--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Zech.2.9">Zec 2:9</reference>). The Divine Angel announces that in what He has just spoken, He has been commissioned by God the Father. <div eID="gen24538" type="x-p"/>
entries.934fc97ff66df4dc4b3d71c9597832c184934a4d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13061"/><div sID="gen24539" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13061"/><hi type="bold">10. who ... despised ... small things--</hi>He reproves their ungrateful unbelief, which they felt because of the humble beginning, compared with the greatness of the undertaking; and encourages them with the assurance that their progress in the work, though small, was an earnest of great and final success, because Jehovah's eye is upon Zerubbabel and the work, to support Him with His favor. Contrast, "great is the day of Jezreel" (<reference osisRef="Hos.1.11">Ho 1:11</reference>) with "the day of small things" here.<div eID="gen24539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24540" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall rejoice ... with those seven; they are the eyes of the Lord--</hi>rather, "they, even those seven eyes of the Lord (compare <reference osisRef="Zech.3.9">Zec 3:9</reference>), which ... shall rejoice and see (that is, rejoicingly see) the plummet (literally, the 'stone of tin') in the hand of Zerubbabel" [Moore]; the plummet in his hand indicating that the work is going forward to its completion. The Hebrew punctuation, however, favors English Version, of which the sense is, They who incredulously "despised" such "small" beginnings of the work as are made now, shall rejoicingly see its going on to completion under Zerubbabel, "with (the aid of) those seven," namely, the "seven eyes upon one stone" (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.9">Zec 3:9</reference>): which are explained, "They are the eyes of the Lord which," &c. [Pembellus]. So differently do men and Jehovah regard the "small" beginnings of God's work (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.12">Ezr 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hag.2.3">Hag 2:3</reference>). Men "despised" the work in its early stage: God rejoicingly regards it, and shall continue to do so.<div eID="gen24540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">run to and fro, &c.--</hi>Nothing in the whole earth escapes the eye of Jehovah, so that He can ward off all danger from His people, come from what quarter it may, in prosecuting His work (<reference osisRef="Prov.15.3">Pr 15:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.9">1Co 16:9</reference>). <div eID="gen24541" type="x-p"/>
entries.4350b57a97d51211e2a0c69faef9f38c65e49c83: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13062"/><div sID="gen24542" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13062"/>11-12. Zechariah three times (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.4">Zec 4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.12">11, 12</reference>) asks as to the two olives before he gets an answer; the question becomes more minute each time. What he at first calls "two olive trees," he afterwards calls "branches," as on closer looking he observes that the "branches" of the trees are the channels through which a continual flow of oil dropped into the bowl of the lamps (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.2">Zec 4:2</reference>), and that this is the purpose for which the two olive trees stand beside the candlestick. Primarily, the "two" refer to Joshua and Zerubbabel. God, says Auberlen, at each of the transition periods of the world's history has sent great men to guide the Church. So the two witnesses shall appear before the destruction of Antichrist. Antitypically, "the two anointed ones" (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.14">Zec 4:14</reference>) are the twofold supports of the Church, the civil power (answering to Zerubbabel) and the ecclesiastical (answering to Joshua, the high priest), which in the restored Jewish polity and temple shall "stand by," that is, minister to "the Lord of the whole earth," as He shall be called in the day that He sets up His throne in Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.9">Zec 14:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.2.44">Da 2:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Re 11:15</reference>). Compare the description of the offices of the "priests" and the "prince" (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.23">Is 49:23</reference>; Eze 44:1-46:24). As in <reference osisRef="Rev.11.3">Re 11:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.4">4</reference>, the "two witnesses" are identified with the two olive trees and the two candlesticks. Wordsworth explains them to mean the Law and the Gospel: the two Testaments that witness in the Church for the truth of God. But this is at variance with the sense here, which requires Joshua and Zerubbabel to be primarily meant. So Moses (the prophet and lawgiver) and Aaron (the high priest) ministered to the Lord among the covenant-people at the exodus; Ezekiel (the priest) and Daniel (a ruler) in the Babylonian captivity; so it shall be in restored Israel. Some think Elijah will appear again (compare the transfiguration, <reference osisRef="Matt.17.3">Mt 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.17.11">11</reference>, with Mal 4:4, 5; <reference osisRef="John.1.21">Joh 1:21</reference>) with Moses. <reference osisRef="Rev.11.6">Re 11:6</reference>, which mentions the very miracles performed by Elijah and Moses (shutting heaven so as not to rain, and turning water into blood), favors this (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.7.19">Ex 7:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.1">1Ki 17:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.4.25">Lu 4:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.16">Jas 5:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.17">17</reference>). The period is the same, "three years and six months"; the scene also is in Israel (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.8">Re 11:8</reference>), "where our Lord was crucified." It is supposed that for the first three and a half years of the hebdomad (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.20-Dan.9.27">Da 9:20-27</reference>), God will be worshipped in the temple; in the latter three and a half years, Antichrist will break the covenant (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Da 9:27</reference>), and set himself up in the temple to be worshipped as God (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4">2Th 2:4</reference>). The witnesses prophesy the former three and a half years, while corruptions prevail and faith is rare (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.8">Lu 18:8</reference>); then they are slain and remain dead three and a half years. Probably, besides individual witnesses and literal years, there is a fulfilment in long periods and general witnesses, such as the Church and the Word, the civil and religious powers so far as they have witnessed for God. So "the beast" in Revelation answers to the civil power of the apostasy; "the false prophet" to the spiritual power. Man needs the priest to atone for guilt, and the prophet-king to teach holiness with kingly authority. These two typically united in Melchisedek were divided between two till they meet in Messiah, the Antitype. <reference osisRef="Zech.6.11-Zech.6.13">Zec 6:11-13</reference> accords with this. The Holy Spirit in this His twofold power of applying to man the grace of the atonement, and that of sanctification, must in one point of view be meant by the two olive trees which supply the bowl at the top of the candlestick (that is, Messiah at the head of the Church); for it is He who filled Jesus with all the fulness of His unction (<reference osisRef="John.3.34">Joh 3:34</reference>). But this does not exclude the primary application to Joshua and Zerubbabel, "anointed" (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.14">Zec 4:14</reference>) with grace to minister to the Jewish Church: and so applicable to the twofold supports of the Church which are anointed with the Spirit, the prince and the priest, or minister. <div eID="gen24542" type="x-p"/>
entries.22d5592c75e43424c4c396c6676ca4cae6a262d5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13064"/><div sID="gen24547" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13064"/><hi type="bold">13. Knowest thou not--</hi>God would awaken His people to zeal in learning His truth. <div eID="gen24547" type="x-p"/>
entries.585f62589f96a2430c24f4b32bbc649510fa7942: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13065"/><div sID="gen24548" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13065"/><hi type="bold">14. anointed ones--</hi>literally, "sons of oil" (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.1">Is 5:1</reference>, Margin). Joshua the high priest, and Zerubbabel the civil ruler, must first be anointed with grace themselves, so as to be the instruments of furnishing it to others (compare <reference osisRef="1John.2.20">1Jo 2:20</reference>, 27). <chapter eID="Zech.4"/>

entries.8ad7f21d73a0df1608a5024dfe8883bd07f25a64: <div eID="gen35478" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen35479" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35480" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35480" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35479" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35481" type="x-p"/> The prophet, overpowered by his last vision, is roused by the angel to behold another, <reference osisRef="Zac.4.1">Zac 4:1</reference>; intended also to assure the Jews of the success of Joshua and Zerubbabel in building the temple, and surmounting every obstacle in the way; till at length, by the good providence of God, it should be finished, amidst the joyful acclamations of the spectators, <reference osisRef="Zac.4.2-Zac.4.10">Zac 4:2-10</reference>. The angel's explanation of the golden candlestick, and of the two olive trees, <reference osisRef="Zac.4.11-Zac.4.14">Zac 4:11-14</reference>.
entries.c6f422710952414db2d4b95d91412b8e61c56728: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen35495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35496" type="x-p"/> A candlestick all of gold - This candlestick is formed in some measure after that of the sanctuary, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.31">Exo 25:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.32">Exo 25:32</reference> : but in that of the sanctuary there was no bowl, nor seven pipes, nor seven lamps, nor the two olive trees. The two olive trees were to supply the bowl with oil; the bowl was to communicate the oil to the seven pipes; and the seven pipes were to supply the seven lamps. In general, the candlestick, its bowl, pipes, lamps, and olive trees, are emblems of the pure service of God, and the grace and salvation to be enjoyed by his true worshippers. The candlestick may, however, represent the whole Jewish state, ecclesiastical and civil; the oil, producing the light, the grace and mercy of God; and the two olive trees, the source of infinite love, whence that grace proceeds. The pipes may signify all means of grace; and the seven lamps, the perfection and abundance of the light and salvation provided. Some may take them in the following way: - <div eID="gen35496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35497" type="x-p"/> 1. The olive trees, the Divine goodness, yield the oil from the olive berry, which is its fruit. <div eID="gen35497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35498" type="x-p"/> 2. From each comes a pipe to convey the oil to the bowl. <div eID="gen35498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35499" type="x-p"/> 3. This oil is collected in the bowl, which is supposed to represent Jesus, the great Mediator, through whom alone all grace and mercy descend to man. <div eID="gen35499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35500" type="x-p"/> 4. The seven pipes, the various means of grace - reading, hearing, prayer, sacraments, etc. - through which Christ dispenses his grace and blessing to his followers. <div eID="gen35500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35501" type="x-p"/> 5. The seven lamps - the Spirit of God in its plentitude of graces, gifts, and light, dispensed to the Christian Church.
entries.489eb0a7e3992063017cb54b375da67b06ee0340: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen35501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35502" type="x-p"/> This is the word of the Lord unto Zerubbabel - This prince was in a trying situation, and he needed especial encouragement from God; and here it is: Not by might, (of thy own), nor by power, (authority from others), but by my Spirit - the providence, authority, power, and energy of the Most High. In this way shall my temple be built; in this way shall my Church be raised and preserved. No secular arm, no human prudence, no earthly policy, no suits at law, shall ever be used for the founding, extension, and preservation of my Church. But the spirit of the world says, "These are all means to which as we must have recourse; otherwise the cause of God may be ruined." Satan, thou liest!  <chapter eID="Zech.4"/> <div eID="gen35502" type="x-p"/>
entries.81936a0ec937356e7cf1d1098a33dc2d158bb534: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen35481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35482" type="x-p"/> O great mountain? - The hinderances which were thrown in the way; the regal prohibition to discontinue the building of the temple. <div eID="gen35482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35483" type="x-p"/> Before Zerubbabel - a plain - The sovereign power of God shall remove them. March on, Zerubbabel; all shall be made plain and smooth before thee. I have given thee the work to do, and I will remove all hinderances out of thy way. <div eID="gen35483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35484" type="x-p"/> He shall bring forth the headstone - As he has laid the foundation stone, so shall he put on the headstone: as he has begun the building, so shall he finish it! <div eID="gen35484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35485" type="x-p"/> With shoutings - The universal acclamation of the people. <div eID="gen35485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35486" type="x-p"/> Grace, grace unto it - How beautiful is this structure! May the favor of God ever rest upon it, and be manifested in it!
entries.7c9f5e52952c46743067fd2bcc36ddc23f8ff63a: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen35486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35487" type="x-p"/> Who hath despised the day of small things? - The poverty, weakness, and unbefriended state of the Jews. It was said, "What do these feeble Jews?" "Will they build," etc.? No. But God will build by them, and perfect his building too. <div eID="gen35487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35488" type="x-p"/> And shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel - He is master builder under God, the grand architect. <div eID="gen35488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35489" type="x-p"/> Those seven - are the eyes of the Lord - Either referring to his particular and especial providence; or to those ministering spirits, whom he has employed in behalf of the Jews, to dispense the blessings of that providence. See <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">2Chr 16:9</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Pro.15.3">Pro 15:3</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Zac.3.9">Zac 3:9</reference> (note).
entries.5d8bc89057fafa3079980778fe59deefc64dcee5: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen35489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35490" type="x-p"/> What are these two olive trees - See on <reference osisRef="Zac.4.2">Zac 4:2</reference> (note).
entries.ea5fece3422c381baf767c15228f3a6fc0bf36f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen35490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35491" type="x-p"/> What be these two olive branches - That is, two boughs laden with branches of olive berries.
entries.ad14e5fa6db573e0dec8bbcc9ae7aae4a7ffb0d9: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen35491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35492" type="x-p"/> These are the two anointed ones - Joshua, the high priest; and Zerubbabel the governor. These are anointed - appointed by the Lord; and stand by him, the one to minister in the ecclesiastical, the other in the civil state. <div eID="gen35492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35493" type="x-p"/> Probably we may not be able to comprehend the whole of this hieroglyphical vision; for even the interpreting angel does not choose to answer the questions relative to this, which were put to him by the prophet. See <reference osisRef="Zac.4.4">Zac 4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zac.4.11">Zac 4:11</reference>. But though the particulars are hard to be understood; yet the general meaning has, I hope, been given. <div eID="gen35493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35494" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen35494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35495" type="x-p"/> The angel - came again, and waked me - Abp. Newcome considers this vision as represented on the same night, <reference osisRef="Zac.1.8">Zac 1:8</reference>, with the preceding ones. See the latter part of <reference osisRef="Zac.1.10">Zac 1:10</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Zac.3.9">Zac 3:9</reference>. After some interval the prophet, overpowered with the vision which had been presented to him, was awakened from his prophetic trance as from a sleep.

entries.1aaabd58377130a5909f17b7143616da0c8ed06f: Zec 4:1-3 <div eID="gen16813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16814" type="x-p"/> Zec 4:1. <hi type="italic">“And the angel that talked with me returned and waked me, like a man who is waked out of his sleep.” </hi> After the prophet has seen four visions one after another, probably with very short intervals, and has heard the marvellous interpretation of them, he is so overpowered by the impression produced by what he has seen and heard, that he falls into a state of spiritual exhaustion resembling sleep, just as Peter and his companions were unable to keep awake at the transfiguration of Christ (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.32">Luk 9:32</reference>). He has not only fallen back into the state of ordinary human consciousness, but his ordinary spiritual consciousness was so depressed that he resembled a man asleep, and had to be waked out of this sleep-like state by the mediating angel, in order to be qualified for further seeing. It is evident from the expression ויּשׁב (and he returned) that the <hi type="italic">angelus interpres</hi> had left the prophet after the termination of the previous visions, and now came back to him again. The fresh vision which presents itself to his spiritual intuition, is described according to its principal features in Zec 4:2 and Zec 4:3. Zec 4:2. <hi type="italic">“And he said to me, What seest thou? And I said, I see, and behold a candlestick all of gold, and its oil-vessel up above it, and its seven lamps upon it, seven pipes each for the lamps upon the top of it.</hi> Zec 4:3. <hi type="italic">And two olive trees </hi>(oil trees) <hi type="italic">by it, one to the right of the oil-vessel, and one to the left of it.”</hi> The second ויאמר (<hi type="italic">chethib</hi>) in Zec 4:2 might, if necessary, be explained in the way proposed by L. de Dieu, Gusset., and Hofmann, viz., by supposing that the mediating angel had no sooner asked the prophet what he saw, than he proceeded, without waiting for his answer, to give a description himself of what was seen. But this is at variance with the analogy of all the rest of the visions, where the visions seen by the prophet are always introduced with ראיתי or ואראה followed by והנּה (cf. Zec 1:8; Zec 2:1, Zec 2:5; Zec 5:1; Zec 6:1), and it remains quite inflexible; so that we must accept the <hi type="italic">keri</hi> ואמר, which is adopted by the early translators, and found in many codd., as being the true reading, and pronounce ויאמר a copyist’s error. On the combination מנורת זהב כּלּהּ, in which the last two words are construed as a relative clause in subordination to <hi type="italic">menōrath</hi>, see Ewald, §§332, <hi type="italic">c</hi>. <div eID="gen16814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16815" type="x-p"/> The visionary candlestick, all of gold, with its seven lamps, is unquestionably a figurative representation of the seven-branched golden candlestick in the tabernacle, and differs from this only in the three following additions which are peculiar to itself: (1) That is has its <hi type="italic">gullâh</hi> (גּלּהּ for גּלּתה, with the feminine termination resolved; cf. Hos 13:2, and Ewald, §257, <hi type="italic">d</hi>), i.e., a can or round vessel for the oil, which was omitted altogether from the candlestick of the holy place, when the lamps were filled with oil by the priests, “at the top of it” (על־ראשׁהּ); (2) That it had seven <hi type="italic">mūtsâqōth</hi> (pipes) each for the lamps, that is to say, tubes through which the oil poured from the <hi type="italic">gullâh</hi> into the lamps, or was conducted to them, whereas the candlestick of the tabernacle had no pipes, but only seven arms (<hi type="italic">qânı̄m</hi>), for the purpose of holding the lamps, which of course could not be wanting in the case of the visionary candlestick, and are merely omitted from the description as being self-evident. The number of the pipes is also a disputed point, viz., whether שׁבעה ושׁבעה means seven and seven, i.e., fourteen, or whether it is to be taken distributively, seven each for the lamps, i.e., seven for each lamp, and therefore forty-nine for the seven. The distributive view is disputed by Hitzig and Koehler as at variance with the usage of the language: the former proposing to alter the text, so as to obtain seven pipes, i.e., one for each lamp; and the latter, on the other hand, assuming that there were fourteen pipes, and inferring from the statement “seven and seven,” instead of fourteen, that the second seven are to be sought in a different place from the first, that is to say, that the first seven led from the oil-vessel to the seven different lamps, whilst the second seven connected the seven lamps with one another, which would have been a very strange and perfectly useless provision. But there is no foundation whatever for the assertion that it is at variance with the usage of the language. For although a distributive relation is certainly expressed as a rule by the simple repetition of the number without any connecting <hi type="italic">Vav</hi>, such passages as <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.20">2Sa 21:20</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.6">1Ch 20:6</reference> show quite indisputably that the repetition of the same number with the <hi type="italic">Vav cop.</hi> between is also to be taken distributively. When, for example, it is stated in <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.20">2Sa 21:20</reference>, with regard to the hero of Gath, that the fingers of his hands and the fingers (toes) of his feet were “<hi type="italic">shēsh vâshēsh</hi>, four-and-twenty in number,” it is evident that <hi type="italic">shēsh vâshēsh</hi> cannot mean “six and six,” because six and six do not make twenty-four; and a division of the <hi type="italic">shēsh</hi> between the hands and feet is also untenable, because his two hands had not six fingers on them, but twelve, and so his two feet had not six toes on them, but twelve. Consequently <hi type="italic">shēsh vâshēsh</hi> must be taken distributively: the fingers of his (two) hands and the toes of his (two) feet were six each; for it is only 2 + 2 (= 4) x 6 that can give 24. This is shown still more clearly in <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.6">1Ch 20:6</reference> : “and his fingers were <hi type="italic">shēsh vâshēsh</hi>, four-and-twenty.” It is in this distributive sense, which is thus thoroughly established, so far as the usage of the language is concerned, that שׁבעה ושׁבעה מוּץ is to be taken: seven pipes each for the lamps, i.e., forty-nine for the seven lamps; inasmuch as if fourteen pipes were meant, it would be impossible to imagine any reason why “seven and seven” should be written instead of fourteen. And we cannot be shaken in this conviction, either by the objection “that if there was any proportion between the pipes and the size of the oil-vessel, such a number of pipes could not possibly (?) spring from one oil-can” (Koehler), or by the statement that “forty-nine would be quite as much at variance with the <hi type="italic">original</hi> as fourteen, since that had only one pipe for every lamp” (Hitzig). For the supposed original for the pipes had no existence, inasmuch as the Mosaic candlestick had no pipes at all; and we can form no opinion as to the possibility of forty-nine pipes issuing from one oil-vessel, because we have no information as to the size either of the oil-vessel or of the pipes. (3) The third peculiarity in the visionary candlestick consists in the olive trees on the right and left of the oil-vessel, which supplied it with oil, and whose connection with the candlestick is first described in Zec 4:12. These three additions which were made to the golden candlestick seen by Zechariah, as contrasted with the golden candlestick of the tabernacle, formed the apparatus through which it was supplied with the oil required to light it continually without the intervention of man.
entries.c998792f994b3d889d68fe8d48e6eb06fcba1e89: Zec 4:4-7 <div eID="gen16815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16816" type="x-p"/> The interpretation of this vision must therefore be founded upon the meaning of the golden candlestick in the symbolism of the tabernacle, and be in harmony with it. The prophet receives, first of all, the following explanation, in reply to his question on this point: Zec 4:4. <hi type="italic">“And I answered and spake to the angel that talked with me, What are these, my lord?</hi> Zec 4:5. <hi type="italic">And the angel that talked with me answered and said to me, Knowest thou not what these are? And I said, No, my lord.</hi> Zec 4:6. <hi type="italic">Then he answered and spake to me thus: This is the word of Jehovah to Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, and not by power, but by my Spirit, saith Jehovah of hosts.</hi> Zec 4:7. <hi type="italic">Who art thou, O great mountain before Zerubbabel? Into a plain! And He will bring out the top-stone amidst shoutings, Grace, grace unto it!” </hi> The question addressed by the prophet to the mediating angel, “What are these?” (<hi type="italic">mâh 'ēlleh</hi>, as in Zec 2:2) does not refer to the two olive trees only (Umbreit, Kliefoth), but to everything described in Zec 4:2 and Zec 4:3. We are not warranted in assuming that the prophet, like every other Israelite, knew what the candlestick with its seven lamps signified; and even if Zechariah had been perfectly acquainted with the meaning of the golden candlestick in the holy place, the candlestick seen by him had other things beside the two olive trees which were not to be found in the candlestick of the temple, viz., the <hi type="italic">gullâh</hi> and the pipes for the lamps, which might easily make the meaning of the visionary candlestick a doubtful thing. And the counter-question of the angel, in which astonishment is expressed, is not at variance with this. For that simply presupposes that the object of these additions is so clear, that their meaning might be discovered from the meaning of the candlestick itself. The angel then gives him the answer in Zec 4:6 : “This (the vision as a symbolical prophecy) is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel: Not by might,” etc. That is to say, through this vision Zerubbabel is informed that it - namely, the work which Zerubbabel has taken in hand or has to carry out - will not be effected by human strength, but by the Spirit of God. The work itself is not mentioned by the angel, but is referred to for the first time in Zec 4:7 in the words, “He will bring out the top-stone,” and then still more clearly described in the word of Jehovah in Zec 4:9 : “The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house (the temple), and his hands will finish it.” It by no means follows from this that the candlestick, with its seven lamps, represented Zerubbabel’s temple (Grotius, Hofmann); for whilst it is impossible that the candlestick, as one article of furniture in the temple, should be a figurative representation of the whole temple, what could the two olive trees, which supplied the candlestick with oil, signify with such an interpretation? Still less can the seven lamps represent the seven eyes of God (Zec 4:10), according to which the candlestick would be a symbol of God or of the Spirit (Hitzig, Maurer, Schegg). The significance of the candlestick in the holy place centred, as I have shown in my <hi type="italic">biblische Archäologie</hi> (i. p. 107), in its seven lamps, which were lighted every evening, and burned through the night. The burning lamps were a symbol of the church or of the nation of God, which causes the light of its spirit, or of its knowledge of God, to shine before the Lord, and lets it stream out into the night of a world estranged from God. As the disciples of Christ were called, as lights of the world (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.14">Mat 5:14</reference>), to let their lamps burn and shine, or, as candlesticks in the world (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.35">Luk 12:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.15">Phi 2:15</reference>), to shine with their light before men (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.16">Mat 5:16</reference>), so as the church of the Old Testament also. The correctness of this explanation of the meaning of the candlestick is placed beyond all doubt by <reference osisRef="Rev.1.20">Rev 1:20</reference>, where the seven λυχνίαι, which John saw before the throne of God, are explained as being the seven ἐκκλησίαι, which represent the new people of God, viz., the Christian church. The candlestick itself merely comes into consideration here as the stand which carried the lamps, in order that they might shine, and as such was the divinely appointed form for the realization of the purpose of the shining lamps. In this respect it might be taken as a symbol of the kingdom of God on its formal side, i.e., of the divinely appointed organism for the perpetuation and life of the church. But the lamps received their power to burn from the oil, with which they had to be filled before they could possibly burn. <div eID="gen16816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16817" type="x-p"/> Oil, regarded according to its capacity to invigorate the body and increase the energy of the vital spirits, is used in the Scriptures as a symbol of the Spirit of God, not in its transcendent essence, but so far as it works in the world, and is indwelling in the church; and not merely the anointing oil, as Kliefoth supposes, but also the lamp oil, since the Israelites had no other oil than olive oil even for burning, and this was used for anointing also.<note placement="foot">The distinction between lamp oil and anointing oil, upon which Kliefoth founds his interpretation of the visionary candlestick, and which he tries to uphold from the language itself, by the assertion that the anointing oil is always called <hi type="italic">shemen</hi>, whereas the lamp oil is called <hi type="italic">yitshâr</hi>, is shown to be untenable by the simple fact that, in the minute description of the preparation of the lamp oil for the sacred candlestick, and the repeated allusion to this oil in the Pentateuch, the term <hi type="italic">yitshâr</hi> is never used, but always <hi type="italic">shemen</hi>, although the word <hi type="italic">yitshâr</hi> is by no means foreign to the Pentateuch, but occurs in Num 18:12; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.13">Deu 7:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.14">Deu 11:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.12.17">Deu 12:17</reference>, and other passages. According to <reference osisRef="Exod.27.20">Exo 27:20</reference>, the lamp oil for the candlestick was to be prepared from <hi type="italic">shemen zayith zâkh kâthı̄th</hi>, pure, beaten olive oil (so also according to <reference osisRef="Lev.24.2">Lev 24:2</reference>); and according to <reference osisRef="Exod.30.24">Exo 30:24</reference>, <hi type="italic">shemen zayith</hi>, olive oil, was to be used for anointing oil. Accordingly the lamp oil for the candlestick is called <hi type="italic">shemen lammâ'ōr</hi> in <reference osisRef="Exod.25.6">Exo 25:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.35.8">Exo 35:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.35.28">Exo 35:28</reference>, and <hi type="italic">shemen hammâ'ōr</hi> in <reference osisRef="Exod.35.14">Exo 35:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.39.37">Exo 39:37</reference>, and Num 4:16; and the anointing oil is called <hi type="italic">shemen hammishchâh</hi> in <reference osisRef="Exod.29.7">Exo 29:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.31.11">Exo 31:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.35.15">Exo 35:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.39.38">Exo 39:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.40.9">Exo 40:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.8.20">Lev 8:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.10">Lev 8:10</reference>, and other passages; and <hi type="italic">shemen miwshchath</hi>-<hi type="italic">qōdesh</hi> in Exo 30:25. Apart from Zec 4:14 of the chapter before us, <hi type="italic">yitshâr</hi> is never used for the lamp oil as such, but simply in the enumeration of the productions of the land, or of the tithes and first-fruits, when it occurs in connection with <hi type="italic">tı̄rōsh</hi>, must or new wine (Num 18:12; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.13">Deu 7:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.14">Deu 11:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.14.23">Deu 14:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.18.4">Deu 18:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.51">Deu 28:51</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.31.5">2Ch 31:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.28">2Ch 32:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.5.11">Neh 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.10.39">Neh 10:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.13.12">Neh 13:12</reference>; Hos 2:9, Hos 2:22; <reference osisRef="Joel.1.10">Joe 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.19">Joe 2:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.2.24">Joe 2:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.12">Jer 31:12</reference>; Hag 1:11), but never in connection with <hi type="italic">yayin</hi> (wine), with which <hi type="italic">shemen</hi> is connected (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.40">1Ch 12:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.2.14">2Ch 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.11">2Ch 11:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.21.17">Pro 21:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.40.10">Jer 40:10</reference>). It is evident from this that <hi type="italic">yitshâr</hi>, the shining, bears the same relation to <hi type="italic">shemen</hi>, fatness, as <hi type="italic">tı̄rōsh</hi>, must, to <hi type="italic">yayin</hi>, wine, - namely, that <hi type="italic">yitshâr</hi> is applied to oil as the juice of the olive, i.e., as the produce of the land, from its shining colour, whilst <hi type="italic">shemen</hi> is the name given to it when its strength and use are considered. Hengstenberg’s opinion, that <hi type="italic">yitshâr</hi> is the rhetorical or poetical name for oil, has no real foundation in the circumstance that <hi type="italic">yitshâr</hi> only occurs once in the first four books of the Pentateuch (Num 18:12) and <hi type="italic">shemen</hi> occurs very frequently; whereas in Deuteronomy <hi type="italic">yitshâr</hi> is used more frequently than <hi type="italic">shemen</hi>, viz., the former six times, and the latter four.</note> <div eID="gen16817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16818" type="x-p"/> And in the case of the candlestick, the oil comes into consideration as a symbol of the Spirit of God. There is no force in Kliefoth’s objection - namely, that inasmuch as the oil of the candlestick was to be presented by the people, it could not represent the Holy Spirit with its power and grace, as coming from God to man, but must rather represent something human, which being given up to God, is cleansed by God through the fire of His word and Spirit; and being quickened thereby, is made into a shining light. For, apart from the fact that the assumption upon which this argument is founded - namely, that in the oil of the candlestick the Spirit of God was symbolized by the altar fire with which it was lighted - is destitute of all scriptural support, since it is not mentioned anywhere that the lamps of the candlestick were lighted with fire taken from the altar of burnt-offering, but it is left quite indefinite where the light or fire for kindling the lamps was to be taken from; apart, I say, from this, such an argument proves too much (<hi type="italic">nimium, ergo nihil</hi>), because the anointing oil did not come directly from God, but was also presented by the people. Supposing, therefore, that this circumstance was opposed to the symbolical meaning of the lamp oil, it would also be impossible that the anointing oil should be a symbol of the Holy Ghost, since not only the oil, but the spices also, which were used in preparing the anointing oil, were given by the people (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.6">Exo 25:6</reference>). We might indeed say, with Kliefoth, that “the oil, as the fatness of the fruit of the olive tree, is the last pure result of the whole of the vital process of the olive tree, and therefore the quintessence of its nature; and that man also grows, and flourishes, and bears fruit like an olive tree; and therefore the fruit of his life’s fruit, the produce of his personality and of the unfolding of his life, may be compared to oil.” But it must also be added (and this Kliefoth has overlooked), that the olive tree could not grow, flourish, and bear fruit, unless God first of all implanted or communicated the power to grow and bear fruit, and then gave it rain and sunshine and the suitable soil for a prosperous growth.
